profiles.name: Hugh Sinclair Williams
profiles.description: Hugh Sinclair Williams was a member of the Philadelphia Black liberation group known as the Revolutionaries. He was arrested at the scene of the August 29, 1970 Cobbs Creek confrontation in which Philadelphia police officer Frank Von Colln was killed and another officer was wounded. Williams and five codefendants were convicted in a joint trial; the Pennsylvania Supreme Court record identifies Williams as one of the defendants and records the group’s revolutionary political context. He received a life sentence. The Prison Activist Resource Center still listed him as a political prisoner in 2008 under Pennsylvania prisoner number AF-2932. His custody status after that roster has not been independently established.
profiles.query: "Hugh Sinclair Williams" Philadelphia Revolutionaries photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Philadelphia Revolutionaries court records located; no captioned portrait verified.

profiles.name: Alvin Joyner
profiles.description: Alvin Joyner was a member of the Philadelphia Black liberation group known as the Revolutionaries and a defendant in the prosecution arising from the August 29, 1970 Cobbs Creek confrontation in which police officer Frank Von Colln was killed. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed Joyner’s first conviction because of prosecutorial misconduct. He was tried again in April 1977, convicted, and sentenced to life imprisonment in February 1979. The Prison Activist Resource Center listed him in 2008 as a political prisoner under Pennsylvania prisoner number AF-4296. His custody status after that roster has not been independently established.
profiles.query: "Alvin Joyner" Philadelphia Cobbs Creek photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Pennsylvania Joyner opinions located. Fictional Designated Survivor character and unlinked veteran rejected.

profiles.name: Robert Joyner
profiles.description: Robert Joyner was a member of the Philadelphia Black liberation group known as the Revolutionaries and one of the defendants convicted after the August 29, 1970 Cobbs Creek confrontation with police. He received life imprisonment for murder plus a consecutive term for explosives offenses. A 2023 report on aging people in Pennsylvania prisons identified Joyner, then 80, as still serving the life sentence at SCI Phoenix and described an effort to obtain compassionate release. His Pennsylvania prisoner number is AF-3793.
profiles.query: "Robert Joyner" Philadelphia SCI Phoenix photograph portrait
profiles.finding: WURD 2023 aging-prisoner coverage is identity-specific lead; unlinked obituary namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: Leonard J. Cohen
profiles.description: Leonard J. Cohen was a staff member of the UFO Coffeehouse, an antiwar gathering place used by soldiers stationed at Fort Jackson in Columbia, South Carolina. Police padlocked the coffeehouse and arrested Cohen and three colleagues on January 13, 1970. Cohen and manager Duane Ferre remained jailed because they could not make $7,500 bail. On April 27, Cohen, Ferre, and William Balk were convicted of maintaining a public nuisance and received extraordinary six-year sentences. The judge released them pending appeal, and the sentences were later reduced in exchange for lifetime banishment from South Carolina.
profiles.query: "Leonard J. Cohen" UFO coffeehouse Columbia photograph portrait
profiles.finding: UFO Coffeehouse-specific search did not establish portrait; no singer Leonard Cohen image accepted.

profiles.name: Delia Gonzalez
profiles.description: A 39-year-old Chicana activist in Del Rio, Texas facing a 13-count federal indictment (up to 65 years) for allegedly inducing Mexican nationals to enter the U.S., a prosecution the paper calls trumped-up. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.2 (1978).
profiles.query: "Delia Gonzalez" Del Rio activist photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Del Rio activist search returned contemporary artist and Mexican official namesakes; rejected.

profiles.name: DeWayne Williams
profiles.description: Cal State Northridge student beaten by LAPD officers and then convicted, by an 11-white jury, of interfering with a police officer; The Black Panther Vol. 14 no.17 (1976) reports he faced up to a year in jail and set up an appeal fund, calling the arrest a racist frame-up.
profiles.finding: April 9 1976 Militant identifies DeWayne Waheeb Williams; scan remains portrait lead.

profiles.name: Douglas Lane
profiles.description: Douglas Lane was one of the "Livernois 5," five young Black men swept up in a Detroit police dragnet after the July 1975 Livernois–Fenkell rebellion and charged in the death of Marian Pyszko, a white autoworker killed by a crowd during the unrest. The uprising had erupted when Andrew Chinarian, the white owner of Bolton's Bar on Livernois Avenue, shot 18-year-old Obie Wynn in the back of the head in his parking lot — a killing for which Chinarian ultimately served only six months on a misdemeanor charge of careless use of a firearm. As the city demanded answers for Pyszko's death, police rounded up young Black men who could be tied to the area; the five defendants were held for about eleven months and tried three times before all of them were acquitted and released.
profiles.finding: University of Michigan Livernois Five exhibit found. British Douglas Lane portrait rejected; captioned exhibit images need inspection.

profiles.name: Earl Brown
profiles.description: Black University of Massachusetts football player convicted in the same 1974 Amherst robbery frame-up as Craemen Gethers; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.25 (1976) reports a community defense movement won him a reduced 3-5 year sentence with work-release.
profiles.finding: UMass case-specific search did not verify portrait; unrelated football media guides not accepted.

profiles.name: Earl Gibson
profiles.description: Earl Gibson was serving a five-years-to-life first-degree-burglary sentence in California beginning in 1965 and became active in prisoner organizing. Prison officials placed Gibson in the San Quentin Adjustment Center after charging him on July 21, 1971 with assaulting an informant and murdering guard Leo Davis. An all-white Marin County jury convicted Gibson and Larry Justice of murder and assault on April 18, 1973. Gibson was then transferred to segregation at Folsom Prison. His custody began before the political prosecution, and the reviewed sources do not establish his final release date.
profiles.query: "Earl Gibson" San Quentin Leo Davis photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives prison newspapers and San Quentin broadcast material found; no individual portrait verified.

profiles.name: Eduardo Cruz
profiles.description: Eduardo “Pancho” Cruz was a Puerto Rican independence activist and pre-law student at City College who founded the student organization PRISA and helped lead the 1968 City College strike. Police arrested him on March 18, 1971. Seven months later, a jury convicted him on six counts involving explosive powder, wristwatch timing devices, and empty cigarette packs. He received a seven-year prison sentence. A February 1973 interview with his defense committee reported that he remained imprisoned at Comstock and had lost sight in one eye while seeking a new trial and bail. His eventual release date remains unresolved.
profiles.query: "Eduardo Cruz" Pancho PRISA City College photograph portrait
profiles.finding: NYU Palante issue64 and contemporary coverage found; Arizona photographer and banking executive namesakes rejected.

profiles.description: Black Vietnam veteran sentenced to life plus five years for an alleged armed bank-robbery kidnapping despite no victim identifying him and no prior record; The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.8 (1977) reports the Eldson McGhee Support Committee seeking his release.

profiles.name: Frank Nubin
profiles.description: Frank Nubin was a 46-year-old Oakland, California steelworker — married, studying structural engineering — who had spent some fifteen years of his life in California prisons and became, to The Black Panther, an emblem of the abuses of the state's indeterminate-sentence and Adult Authority parole system. Arrested at Christmas 1968 with less than a month left on parole (on his former common-law wife's claim that he had attacked her), he was returned to San Quentin on a parole violation in February 1969. In November 1971, after a deputy attorney general called him "a potentially dangerous man," a court ordered him back to prison for ten more months. Documented in The Black Panther (November 29, 1971).
profiles.query: "Frank Nubin" Oakland San Quentin1971 photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Historic Images holds captioned1971 San Quentin press photo; original credit and usable asset verification pending.

profiles.name: Frank Shuford
profiles.description: Frank Norris Shuford was a 22-year-old Black community organizer in Santa Ana, California. Prosecutors charged him after a nonfatal 1972 shooting that occurred while he was at home with family and friends. His first trial ended with a hung jury. An all-white jury convicted him at a second trial in 1974 of assault with intent to commit murder, and he received a 30-year prison sentence. Supporters argued that the prosecution was retaliation for his community organizing and that the evidence did not establish his guilt. His exact admission and release dates remain unresolved.
profiles.query: "Frank Shuford" Santa Ana organizer photograph portrait
profiles.finding: ABAA defense pamphlet and WorldCat newsletter found; portrait scan lead pending.

profiles.name: Gerald Bernard Best
profiles.description: Gerald Bernard Best was 18 when he survived a 1976 Houston police shooting during a car chase that killed his brother Allan Charles Best and Overtone Wayne Ellis. Best was wounded and hospitalized. Police then charged him and fellow survivor Elton Rankin with five counts each of attempted capital murder of a police officer, although witnesses said the occupants had fired no shots. The contemporary report does not establish Best’s booking or release dates or the final disposition.
profiles.finding: Houston1976 case-specific search did not establish portrait.

profiles.name: Glanton Dowdell
profiles.description: Glanton Dowdell was a Detroit artist and Black labor organizer associated with the League of Revolutionary Black Workers. He had spent years in Michigan prisons before becoming known for the Black Madonna mural at Detroit’s Shrine of the Black Madonna. Dowdell moved to Sweden in 1969 while facing a federal savings-bond forgery prosecution. Swedish police arrested him in 1971 on the United States’ extradition request, but the Stockholm District Court rejected the prosecutor’s request to keep him detained and released him. The exact arrest and release dates have not been located. Dowdell remained in Sweden until his death in January 2000.
profiles.query: "Glanton Dowdell" Detroit artist Sweden photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Verified artist-site portrait, matched Detroit/Sweden biography, cropped and deployed.

profiles.name: Gregory Felix
profiles.description: Gregory Felix was arrested by Oakland police vice-squad officers inside an NAACP office in 1979 in connection with the investigation of the killing of officer Melvin Black. The available contemporary report does not state the specific charge, exact arrest or release date, or final disposition, and later sources located in this review did not resolve those details.
profiles.finding: Oakland NAACP1979-specific search did not establish portrait.

profiles.name: Hayward Brown
profiles.description: Detroit Black youth who, with two friends, fought Detroit's notorious STRESS police unit; captured after a massive manhunt and tried, he was acquitted after attorney Ken Cockrel put the police on trial. The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.3 (1978).
profiles.finding: University of Michigan STRESS manhunt exhibit and documentary project found; captioned image lead pending.

profiles.name: Herbert X. Blyden
profiles.description: Herbert X. Blyden was a jailhouse lawyer, prison organizer, and civil-rights activist born in St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands. While imprisoned on a disputed 1965 armed-robbery conviction, he served as a negotiator during the 1970 uprising at the Manhattan House of Detention and as a chief negotiator and spokesman during the September 1971 Attica uprising. State forces beat and tortured Blyden after retaking Attica. Charges arising from both uprisings were dismissed, and he was released in 1973. Blyden later spoke at political and civil-rights rallies and joined the federal civil action brought by Attica survivors. He died from prostate cancer in Buffalo on September 21, 1997.
profiles.finding: NYS archive and contemporary Attica coverage found; portrait/caption inspection pending.

profiles.name: Hercules Anderson
profiles.description: Hercules Anderson was one of four Black land-reclamation protesters arrested by federal marshals at Harris Neck, Georgia, on May 1, 1979. The protesters occupied land that the federal government had taken from a Black community during World War II and refused an order to leave. A federal judge convicted them of criminal contempt on May 4 and imposed thirty days in jail. They spent more than fifteen days in the Savannah jail, but their exact release dates and the amount of the thirty-day sentence ultimately served have not been located.
profiles.finding: Washington Post1979 Harris Neck arrest coverage corroborates case; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Howard Ay Gibbs
profiles.description: Camden, New Jersey Black community anti-drug organizer serving a maximum 80-year sentence at Trenton State Prison after an all-white jury convicted him of murdering a white man; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.27 (1976) reports the Howard Ay Gibbs Defense Committee's charge that the conviction rested on forged testimony and destroyed transcripts.
profiles.query: "Howard Ay Gibbs" Camden Trenton photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Camden Trenton-specific query did not establish portrait.

profiles.name: J.B. Johnson
profiles.description: Black St. Louis man facing a life term for the murder of a policeman during a 1970 robbery, in a case his supporters and attorney William Kunstler called a frame-up built on suppressed evidence; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.8 (1976) reports the National Committee To Free J.B. Johnson.
profiles.query: "J.B. Johnson" St Louis Kunstler photograph portrait

profiles.name: James Barrett
profiles.description: James W. Barrett was convicted of the October 4, 1975 armed robbery of the Northeast Bank's Lunts Corner branch in Portland, Maine — a holdup carried out with Raymond Levasseur, Thomas Manning, and Joseph Aceto of the Sam Melville/Jonathan Jackson Unit, who framed such robberies as political "expropriations." Barrett, who knew Manning from prison, was recruited for the robbery but, by his own court testimony, was then asked to join the group's wider campaign of bombings, kidnappings, and robberies and refused — so he is best understood as a one-time accomplice rather than a committed member of the clandestine cell. He was convicted of armed bank robbery (United States v. Barrett, 766 F.2d 609) and sentenced to a long federal prison term.
profiles.finding: Federal Barrett opinion matches Portland robbery; Liverpool historical subject, archaeologist and photographer namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: James Carrington
profiles.description: James Carrington was a young Black man convicted in 1970 in Appomattox, Virginia of raping a white friend and sentenced to 75 years — a conviction his supporters, organized as a Prisoners Solidarity Committee, said was a frame-up. By 1974, having served four years, he won an argument before the U.S. Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals that there had been racial discrimination in the selection of the all-white jury of twelve elderly men that had convicted him. Documented in The Black Panther (May 11, 1974).
profiles.finding: Appomattox1970-specific search did not verify portrait. NPG historical James Carrington not accepted.

The uprising had erupted when Andrew Chinarian, the white owner of Bolton's Bar on Livernois Avenue, shot 18-year-old Obie Wynn in the back of the head in his parking lot — a killing for which Chinarian ultimately served only six months on a misdemeanor charge of careless use of a firearm. profiles.name: Jay Weiner
profiles.description: Jay Weiner was a roughly 20-year-old aspiring sportswriter and Temple University student who was taken to the Pennsylvania farmhouse where Symbionese Liberation Army fugitive Patty Hearst had been hiding. Subpoenaed on May 19, 1976 before the federal grand jury in Scranton investigating the harboring of Hearst and William and Emily Harris, he refused to testify and was jailed for contempt — by his own account about four months in federal prison (United States v. Weiner, 418 F. Supp. 941). He went on to a long career as a Minneapolis Star Tribune sportswriter and wrote a memoir, A More Dangerous Game.
profiles.finding: Verified own-author-site headshot linked to Hearst-imprisonment memoir; cropped and deployed.

profiles.name: Jogues Egan
profiles.description: Sister Jogues Egan was a Roman Catholic nun and educator jailed for civil contempt in 1971 for refusing to testify before the federal grand jury in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania that investigated the Catholic antiwar left — the so-called East Coast Conspiracy to Save Lives, the alleged plot associated with Daniel and Philip Berrigan to raid draft boards and symbolically kidnap national security adviser Henry Kissinger. Egan refused to answer the grand jury questions on the ground that they were derived from illegal government wiretapping and electronic surveillance. Held in contempt by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and ordered jailed until she testified or the grand jury expired, she carried her challenge to the Supreme Court, which in Gelbard v. United States (1972) upheld the right of grand jury witnesses to refuse to answer questions based on unlawful surveillance. Her resistance, alongside fellow Catholic activist Anne Walsh, made her a prominent figure of Catholic antiwar grand jury resistance.
profiles.finding: Pacifica Harrisburg rally archive and Catholic Left history found; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Larry Justice
profiles.description: Larry Justice was already imprisoned in California by 1967 on sentences for grand auto theft and assault with a deadly weapon, with a federal bank-robbery hold also reported. He was confined in San Quentin’s Adjustment Center beginning in July 1971. Prison officials charged Justice and Earl Gibson on July 21, 1971 with assaulting an informant and murdering guard Leo Davis. An all-white Marin County jury convicted them of murder and assault on April 18, 1973. The reviewed sources do not establish Justice’s final release date.
profiles.query: "Larry Justice" San Quentin Gibson photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives Anvil and1973 prison reporting found; actor namesake rejected.

profiles.name: LaSaunders Hudson
profiles.description: LaSaunders Hudson was a Memphis dry-cleaning business owner who refused to pay state taxes as a protest against the uncompensated oppression of Black people. On June 15, 1972 he disarmed four revenue agents at his shop, made three leave without their clothes and held the fourth while demanding to meet Governor Winfield Dunn. After an eight-hour standoff Hudson met the governor and was taken into custody. He spent the night in the Memphis jail and was released on $2,000 bond on June 16. A kidnapping accusation was dropped, leaving a charge of assault with intent to murder; the final disposition has not been located.
profiles.finding: UNT June16 1972 newspaper and historical tax protest account found; modern tax preparer not identity-confirmed.

profiles.name: Marvin Fentis
profiles.description: Marvin Fentis was a Black Texan who, The Black Panther reported, was already serving two life sentences for defending himself against two Garland, Texas police officers when, in August 1974, he was brought to Houston, tried, and convicted of the murder of a Houston police officer — and sentenced to 38 more years on what his defense attorney, Grey Washington, called purely circumstantial evidence, after police "concentrated on finding three Black men" to fit a fabricated description. Documented in The Black Panther (August 31, 1974).
profiles.finding: Texas Fentis appeal and contemporary Panther scan found; no individual portrait verified.

profiles.name: Marvin Smith
profiles.description: Marvin Smith was a California prisoner, transferred from Soledad to San Quentin, who became a figure in the prison movement. He was charged with assault with a deadly weapon and with holding guards hostage but was acquitted by a jury; San Quentin officials nonetheless kept him locked in a maximum-security adjustment center. In 1971 he filed suit in U.S. District Court to bar the prison from punishing him for acts of which a jury had acquitted him. The underlying incident, per The Black Panther, was his stepping in to break up a fight between a guard and another inmate, Johnny Miller — who had witnessed a guard's misconduct and refused a payoff.
profiles.finding: Contemporary Panther1971 and Anvil prison sources found; photographer Marvin Smith and BYU subject rejected.

profiles.name: Marvin Wilson
profiles.description: Marvin Wilson was jailed in Winston-Salem, North Carolina after city police, led by Officer R.A. Spillman, forced their way into the Long family home and beat its occupants with nightsticks. Marvin Wilson, fifteen years old and a friend of the family, had been in the kitchen with Mrs. Long when the police attacked. Benny Long, his mother, and Marvin Wilson were taken to jail and charged with disorderly conduct, cursing and abusing police officers, and assault upon police officers; Benny (whose back was badly injured) and Marvin both needed hospital treatment. Documented in The Black Panther (December 25, 1971).
profiles.finding: Winston Salem1971 search did not verify portrait; modern football player rejected.

profiles.name: Naomi Burns
profiles.description: Naomi Burns was among the New York activists subpoenaed in 1975 by a grand jury investigating underground political movements. She challenged the subpoenas with other witnesses. The Appellate Division vacated a stay on November 6, 1975, and later movement records identify her as a grand-jury resister. The records located do not establish that Burns was jailed or provide custody dates.
profiles.finding: Grand-jury1975-specific search did not verify portrait; unrelated archive photo not accepted.

profiles.name: Norma Gist
profiles.description: Norma Gist was a thirty-year-old Black mother of two in Idabel, Oklahoma, whose prosecution grew out of an incident in which she criticized a white school principal, Wilfred Conant, for the brutal beating of her ten-year-old son, Sol. On April 12, 1971, after what The Black Panther called a "quickie, non-peer jury trial," she was convicted and sentenced to ten years in the state prison, then released two days later on a $10,000 appeal bond. On November 15, 1971 Idabel and Oklahoma state police seized her from her home and, on November 17, took her to McAlester prison; the state had also cut off her welfare in an effort to force her into submission. Documented in The Black Panther (November 29, 1971).
profiles.finding: Oklahoma Gist v State and Oklahoma Eagle1971 coverage corroborate case; Mississippi/Texas obituaries not linked.

profiles.name: Omar Seku
profiles.description: Omar Seku was one of the Attica Brothers — the prisoners the state of New York prosecuted after the September 1971 uprising at Attica Correctional Facility, which was crushed when state forces retook the prison and killed 29 inmates and 10 hostages. He spent some two years in solitary confinement after being accused of kidnapping a guard, Franklin Kline, and stabbing an inmate, Ronald Lyons — accusations the prosecution abandoned after both Kline and Lyons told reporters the stabbing never happened and that Seku had in fact helped protect the guard. As The Black Panther reported (February 1, 1975), the Attica Brothers' defense, led by William Kunstler and former U.S. Attorney General Ramsey Clark, won a string of pretrial rulings exposing the weakness of the state's cases; most of the 42 indictments against 62 men were ultimately dismissed, and Governor Hugh Carey closed out the prosecutions and granted clemencies in 1976.
profiles.finding: Attica newspaper scans found; no captioned portrait verified.

profiles.name: Patrick Croy
profiles.description: Patrick Hooty Croy was a Shasta Indian sentenced to death for the 1978 shooting death of a Yreka, California police officer following a confrontation that escalated into a hillside shootout. Croy, his sister Norma Jean Croy, and several cousins were prosecuted; Patrick was convicted of first-degree murder in 1979 and sent to death row. In 1985 the California Supreme Court overturned his conviction. At his 1990 retrial, defended by attorney Tony Serra with a landmark defense rooted in the history of violence against Native people, Croy testified that he had acted in self-defense and was acquitted — after roughly twelve years in prison, seven of them on death row. His sister Norma Jean, also convicted in the case, was not released until 1997.
profiles.finding: National Registry of Exonerations case and captioned Norma Jean/Patrick photograph found; clean crop and image quality pending.

profiles.name: Philip Allen
profiles.description: Philip L. Allen was a 20-year-old Los Angeles City College student arrested on January 1, 1975 after Los Angeles County sheriff’s deputies beat him during a confrontation in which one deputy was killed and two were wounded by gunfire. Allen maintained that he never took the deputy’s gun. He spent 67 days in county jail before his March 5 release on bail. A jury later convicted him of voluntary manslaughter and two counts of assault with a deadly weapon on an officer. On October 2, 1975, he received a five-years-to-life sentence; the judge initially continued bail pending appeal but revoked it later that day after learning that Allen had spoken publicly in his own defense. His eventual release date remains unresolved.
profiles.finding: June1975 Militant and Workers Vanguard case coverage found; nineteenth-century senator portrait rejected.

profiles.name: Roderick Kirby
profiles.description: Roderick Lionell Kirby was an 18-year-old Wilmington, North Carolina civil-rights activist arrested after an October 1, 1971 confrontation with police. He was accused of striking Officer W. R. Pearson while officers questioned two youths outside a school event. Kirby was acquitted of resisting an officer but convicted of assaulting a public officer after a December 1971 trial. The North Carolina Court of Appeals upheld the conviction in 1972. Contemporary movement reporting says he received a prison sentence, but the appellate record does not state its length or establish custody dates.
profiles.finding: Kojo Nantambu oral history and contemporary Wilmington movement sources found; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Roger Champen
profiles.description: Roger Champen was one of the Attica Brothers — prisoners indicted after the September 1971 uprising at New York's Attica prison and its bloody suppression, in which the state killed dozens of inmates and hostages. A leader during the rebellion, he became an assistant coordinator of the Attica Legal Defense Committee and himself faced a three-count murder indictment, among the scores of charges (ranging from murder to "possession of prison keys") that Governor Nelson Rockefeller's special grand jury handed down against the prisoners — while the officials responsible for the retaking of the prison went uncharged. The Attica prosecutions of the inmates were eventually largely abandoned, and in 1976 Governor Hugh Carey closed the books on the cases. Documented in The Black Panther (December 8, 1973).
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives We Are Attica, NYS archives and scholarly photo lead found; individual identification pending.

profiles.description: Black man imprisoned at the Deer Island House of Correction for defending himself and his baby daughter during a wave of white racist attacks on Black families in East Boston; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.17 (1976) reports a pattern of police jailing the Black victims rather than their attackers.

profiles.name: Shango Bahati Kakawana
profiles.description:
Shango Bahati Kakawana (Bernard Stroble) was one of the Attica Brothers, indicted on murder and kidnapping charges over the stabbing deaths of two inmates in the prison yard during the September 1971 uprising — among the most serious of the Attica prosecutions. During the September 1971 uprising at New York's Attica prison — in which inmates seized the facility and held hostages for four days before Governor Nelson Rockefeller ordered an armed assault that killed 39 men — the state, in December 1972, indicted 62 surviving inmates on some 1,289 counts while charging no trooper or guard; the Attica Brothers Legal Defense organized their cases, and Governor Hugh Carey closed the inmate prosecutions in 1976. After a closely watched trial he was acquitted of all charges.

One of the 'Attica Brothers,' tried on murder and kidnapping charges arising from the 1971 Attica rebellion; The Black Panther Vol. 14 (1975) reports he was acquitted after the court found the alleged kidnapping never took place.

profiles.name: Tommy Atwood
profiles.description: Tommy Atwood was arrested on March 6, 1972 with the Reverend Benjamin Chavis and Marvin Patrick and accused of conspiring to murder Harvey Cumber during the February 1971 racial violence in Wilmington, North Carolina. Atwood remained jailed through the March 30 probable-cause hearing and was released on bail with the other Wilmington defendants on June 16, 1972. The reviewed records do not establish a later conviction or custodial sentence in the Cumber case.
profiles.finding: DOJ Wilmington hearing and movement-history sources corroborate context; unlinked Tom Atwood obituary rejected.

profiles.name: Wilbur Shabazz
profiles.description: One of the 'Smyrna 7' convicted of escape-related charges at the Delaware Correctional Center; The Black Panther Vol. 15 no.29 (1976) reports the defense committee's charge that the attacks on him were tied to his ideology and politics.
profiles.finding: Masjid Muhammad DCC litigation found; no individual portrait verified.

profiles.name: Willie E. Smith
profiles.description: Willie E. Smith was the defendant in the first of the Attica Brothers cases to reach trial — the prosecutions the state brought against inmates after the September 1971 uprising at New York's Attica Correctional Facility. As The Black Panther reported (October 19, 1974), New York State Supreme Court Justice Frank F. Barger, sitting in Buffalo, dismissed the two counts of sodomy and two counts of sexual abuse the state had charged against Smith — who had been accused of attacking another prisoner during the rebellion — making his the first of the Attica indictments to collapse at trial. He was represented by Rochester attorney James L. Kemp.
profiles.finding: Attica1974-specific search yielded unrelated genealogies/directories; no identity-linked portrait verified.
